summary.text: A protostar is a very young star that is still gathering mass from its parent molecular cloud, and it is the earliest phase of stellar evolution.
The phase begins when a molecular cloud fragment collapses under self-gravity and an opaque core forms, and it ends when the infalling gas is depleted.
A protostar gets its energy from radiation at shocks on its surface and disk, not from hydrogen fusing at its center, and dust makes it radiate in the infrared and millimeter regimes.

facts.label: Length of phase
facts.value: About 500,000 years for a low-mass star

facts.label: Modern picture
facts.value: First suggested by Chushiro Hayashi in 1966

facts.label: Deuterium fusion
facts.value: Predicted to fuse with hydrogen-1, making helium-3

items.prompt: A candle sits inside a thick shade that soaks up its light and gives off only warmth. Why does a protostar resemble that to a visible-light telescope?

options.label: Its surface is too cold to emit any radiation
Dust around it absorbs its light and re-emits it at longer wavelengths
It is hidden behind a younger, brighter star
It gives off only X-rays, which optical telescopes miss

items.explain: The dust absorbs all photons and reradiates them at longer wavelengths, so a protostar is not detectable at optical wavelengths.

items.prompt: A protostar glows even though its center is not yet fusing hydrogen. Where does its energy come from?

options.label: Radiation released at shocks on its surface and on its disk
Reflected sunlight from nearby ordinary stars
Radioactive decay deep in its core
Heat from a black hole hidden inside it

items.explain: Protostars generate energy from the radiation liberated at the shocks on their surface and on the surface of the surrounding disk.

items.prompt: Next to an ordinary star like the Sun, what is a protostar still doing?

options.label: Burning hydrogen into helium at its center
Shedding its outer layers in a supernova
Gathering mass from its parent molecular cloud
Orbiting a brighter star it feeds on

items.explain: A protostar is a very young star that is still gathering mass from its parent molecular cloud.

items.prompt: Gas keeps falling toward a young dense core, but more and more of it lands on a surrounding disk instead of on the young star. What explains that?

options.label: A strong magnetic field repels the gas from the star
A consequence of angular momentum conservation
The disk is hotter than the star, so it pulls harder
The star has already finished growing

items.explain: As the collapse continues, an increasing amount of gas impacts the disk rather than the star, a consequence of angular momentum conservation.

items.prompt: A young object has finished gathering gas from its surroundings and is slowly contracting. What do astronomers call it now?

options.label: A pre-main-sequence star
A white dwarf
A fresh molecular cloud fragment
A planet in a disk

items.explain: The protostar phase ends when the infalling gas is depleted, leaving a pre-main-sequence star.

items.prompt: Astronomers commonly label Class 0 and Class I sources as protostars. How firm is the evidence for that identification?

options.label: It is proven by direct visible-light images
It is commonly believed, but there is still no definitive evidence
It has been ruled out, since they are ordinary stars
It has never been studied at all

items.explain: It is commonly believed that Class 0 or Class I sources are protostars, but there is still no definitive evidence for this identification.
